If the diagonals of a square increase at a rate of $9\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\text{/s}$, at what rate is the perimeter changing?

examples.knowledge_point: Relating the Rate of Change of a Diagonal Length to Another Rate of Change
examples.problem: The sides of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to twice the rate of increase of the diagonal. What is the area of the square at that moment?
examples.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

Using implicit differentiation and the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 2\dfrac{\textrm d h}{\textrm d t}$, so replacing $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm dt}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 2\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 2 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have $h=2,$ and therefore the area of the square at that moment is

$$
A = \dfrac{2^2}{2} = 2.
$$

feedback.problem: The area of a square increases at a rate of $4{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ At what rate are the lengths of the sides of the square increasing when the sides are $1\text{ m}$ long?
feedback.worked_solution:
Here, the area is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

First, let's draw a diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/e920b14f0a8c3e16c4108da5b252721c7751b7ae978b8d4740445c7087c169c6.png)

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =4\text{ m}{}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when the sides are $1\,\text{m},$ we have $x=1.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, the lengths of the sides are increasing at a rate of $2\,\text{m/s}.$
